name: Nickel-zinc
plain: A rechargeable AA at 1.6 volts, closer to the 1.5 volts of a single-use battery than NiMH. It needs its own charger.
self_discharge: At least 60% of capacity retained after 28 days (PKCELL AA datasheet)
summary: Nickel-zinc batteries pair a nickel positive electrode with a zinc negative in an alkaline electrolyte for 1.6 to 1.65V nominal, closer to a single-use battery's 1.5V than NiMH or NiCd. They are sold in AA size for devices that run poorly on 1.2V rechargeables.
body:
## How it works

A nickel-zinc battery is similar to nickel-cadmium: it uses an alkaline electrolyte and a nickel positive electrode, but the negative electrode is zinc. Zinc's tendency to dissolve as zincate and not fully return to the electrode during recharge, along with electrode shape change and dendrite growth, long limited cycle life, and dendrites often shorted the battery. Wikipedia attributes the chemistry's recent viability to stabilized zinc electrodes developed since 2000, improved separators, zinc stabilizers and electrolyte additives such as phosphates. The batteries contain no mercury, lead, cadmium or metal hydrides, and no flammable active materials or organic electrolytes.

## Discharge behavior

The discharge curve resembles NiCd and NiMH but sits higher. Sources give 1.6V (Wikipedia, PKCELL) or 1.65V (Battery University) nominal, and Wikipedia gives an open-circuit voltage of 1.85V when fully charged; PKCELL's AA datasheet specifies more than 1.8V after charge. PKCELL rates its AA at 1500mAh at 300mA, with a 1.3V cutoff at currents below 750mA and 1.2V at higher currents, and for discharge from −20 to 65°C. Battery University gives a specific energy of about 100Wh/kg and 200 to 300 cycles; PKCELL specifies more than 200 cycles, and Wikipedia reports newer batteries with up to 800 cycles. PKCELL's datasheet lists at least 60% of capacity retained after 28 days of storage.

Charging differs from nickel-metal hydride. Battery University and PKCELL both specify charging to 1.9V per cell (constant current, then constant voltage in PKCELL's case), and both Battery University and Wikipedia state that trickle charging is not recommended. PKCELL rates charging from 0 to 45°C. A NiZn battery therefore needs a charger designed for it.

## Uses

Wikipedia describes the higher voltage as particularly suitable for electronic products that require the 1.5V of alkaline single-use batteries rather than the 1.2V of most rechargeable batteries. Battery University notes that the chemistry is available in AA format. Wikipedia describes high-drain performance and notes interest in larger batteries as an alternative to lead-acid.

## History

Thomas Edison received US patent 684204 for a rechargeable nickel-zinc battery in 1901. The Irish chemist James J. Drumm later developed the battery for four two-car Drumm railcar sets that ran on the Dublin to Bray line between 1932 and 1949. Early nickel-zinc batteries gave only a small number of cycles.

## Status

Current, as a niche rechargeable. The sources consulted do not give an IEC designation for nickel-zinc batteries.
strengths: 1.6 to 1.65V nominal, near the 1.5V of single-use batteries
No cadmium, mercury or lead; nickel and zinc are recyclable
limitations: Needs a dedicated charger: 1.9V charge limit and no trickle charge
Cycle life of about 200 to 300 cycles (Battery University)
High self-discharge: PKCELL specifies at least 60% retained after 28 days
safety: Charge only in a charger designed for nickel-zinc; trickle charging is not recommended
